content: 1. Discussions between patients and healthcare providers about reasons to avoid initiating hepatitis B treatment were reported as follows: 17% of respondents had extensive discussions, 20% had moderate discussions, 25% had minimal discussions, and 38% had no discussions at all. 2. When asked if healthcare providers explained the available treatment options for hepatitis B, 39% of respondents said yes, 48% said no, and 13% could not recall. 3. Regarding whether healthcare providers inquired about the patient’s willingness to start hepatitis B treatment, 44% of respondents said yes, 50% said no, and 6% could not remember. 4. A significant majority (85%) of respondents expressed a desire for their healthcare providers to involve them in decision-making about their hepatitis B management and treatment. Only 6% did not want to be involved, and 9% had no preference. 5. Preferences for hepatitis B testing locations were as follows: 59% preferred testing in a hospital, 35% in a laboratory, 29% with a general practitioner or primary care provider, 20% using a self-test at a location of their choice, 13% at a community-based organization, and 8% at a pharmacy. Notably, only 4% preferred testing at an HIV clinic, and 8% had no preference. 6. A majority of individuals (83%) were open to using telehealth or telemedicine for counseling and management of hepatitis B. However, 10% were unsure, and 2% had no preference. 7. Key considerations for hepatitis B testing included convenience of location (54%), the doctor’s knowledge of hepatitis B (53%), direct costs (43%), a non-judgmental atmosphere (26%), waiting time (22%), the ability to remain anonymous (20%), service hours (16%), the presence of community-friendly health professionals (15%), and community or peer support (9%). 8. Confidentiality of test results was the most important factor for individuals receiving a hepatitis B diagnosis (68%), followed by knowledgeable health facility staff (56%), access to counseling (49%), cost of the visit (45%), non-stigmatizing staff (40%), and convenience (26%). 9. After testing positive for hepatitis B, 50% of individuals preferred to start treatment based on their doctor’s recommendation, while 29% preferred to start treatment on the same day. 10. Survey participants emphasized the importance of convenience and cost in both testing and treatment for hepatitis B. They also highlighted the need for confidentiality and knowledgeable staff who can provide appropriate counseling. 11. Barriers to accessing standard hepatitis B care included the cost and accessibility of HBV DNA testing and routine liver enzyme monitoring. Simplifying guidelines and creating alternatives to DNA testing could reduce these barriers. 12. Pregnant individuals with hepatitis B face unique challenges. Trust in healthcare workers, familial support, and improved awareness of the disease and treatment options were identified as facilitators of adherence to antiviral therapy. Barriers included pill size, social stigma, and low hepatitis B knowledge. 13. In resource-limited settings, the availability of HBV diagnostics is severely lacking. For example, only 50% of settings in sub-Saharan Africa reported access to HBV serology and molecular testing. Routine anti-HDV testing among HBsAg-positive individuals was reported in only 20% of settings globally, with even lower rates in sub-Saharan Africa (5%). 14. Tenofovir was the most widely available antiviral drug globally. Healthcare workers prioritized treating individuals with chronic hepatitis B and advanced hepatic fibrosis (stage 3 or 4) as the top priority for antiviral therapy. 15. Among healthcare workers surveyed, 46% reported that children under 18 with chronic hepatitis B were offered antiviral therapy at their facility, while 31% were unsure, and 22% stated that such therapy was not offered. 16. Increasing HBV screening, diagnosis, and strategies to prevent mother-to-child transmission (MTCT) were identified as the highest priorities for hepatitis B elimination, followed by increasing access to antiviral therapy. 17. The survey highlighted significant regional disparities in the availability of diagnostic tests, with sub-Saharan Africa reporting the lowest availability of HBV molecular and serological testing. 18. A high proportion of healthcare workers (82%) agreed that a point-of-care test for HBeAg would add value to hepatitis B care in their settings. 19. The survey results underscore the need for improved access to diagnostics, affordable treatment options, and simplified guidelines to enhance hepatitis B care, particularly in resource-limited settings.
